classification.difficultyReason: The blanks cue standard facts. The hardest decisions are placing the result and index in the logarithmic equation and recognising the y-axis reflection from −x.

questions.mappingNote: The definition and conditions govern the question as a whole. Part (b) assesses conversion and part (f) assesses exponential reflection.
questions.methodNote: The question cues the definition of a logarithm, the restrictions on its base and argument, and its inverse relationship with the exponential function. Part (f) cues the graph transformation obtained by replacing x with −x.

classification.difficultyReason: Students recognise the standard values and apply the inverse identities directly, identifying x > 0 when the logarithm is applied first.

questions.mappingNote: Parts (a) and (b) apply the logarithm definition to the powers 1 and 0. Parts (c) and (d) apply the inverse identities, including the restriction on the logarithm's input.
questions.methodNote: Read each logarithm as the index required to obtain its argument. Use the inverse relationship in both orders with the corresponding domain.

classification.difficultyReason: Students use the inverse relationship to match domain with range in both directions. The first letters cue the terms.

questions.mappingNote: Both parts compare the exponential and logarithmic functions by matching the domain of each to the range of the other.
questions.methodNote: Use the exchange of inputs and outputs when a function is inverted.

classification.difficultyReason: Students apply one conversion rule independently, keeping the base, moving the logarithm's value into the exponent and writing its argument as the result.

questions.mappingNote: All six parts ask for index form, including zero, fractional and negative indices.
questions.methodNote: In a conversion from logarithmic form to index form, retain the base, use the logarithm's value as the index and use its argument as the result.

classification.difficultyReason: Use the given base, result and index to write the equivalent logarithmic equation. Fractional and negative indices require the same conversion.

questions.mappingNote: All six parts ask for logarithmic form, including fractional and negative indices and exact fractional and decimal arguments.
questions.methodNote: In a conversion from index form to logarithmic form, keep the base, place the result in the logarithm's argument and place the index on the other side of the equals sign.

classification.difficultyReason: Rewrite each equation in index form, then choose how to isolate the unknown. The hardest parts undo a negative or fractional power and use the positive-base condition where two algebraic roots are possible.

questions.mappingNote: Index-to-log conversion is assessed through its reverse, with the logarithm definition supplying the equivalence and positive-base condition.
questions.methodNote: The stem explicitly requires rewriting each equation in index form before solving for the exponent, base or argument.

classification.difficultyReason: Find six powers of 2, plot the resulting pairs at their unequal horizontal intervals and use the known logarithmic shape to sketch the curve toward its vertical asymptote.

questions.mappingNote: The linked graph construction is the most advanced assessed task. Finding the outputs uses the logarithm definition.
questions.methodNote: The table and the word ‘Hence’ specify a table-to-graph construction. Read the logarithms as exponents and use the corresponding ordered pairs to sketch the curve.

classification.difficultyReason: Coordinate intercepts, curve order and asymptotic behaviour on common axes, then use the inverse relationship to sketch the logarithmic curve on the same axes as its exponential.

questions.mappingNote: The shared axes assess curve comparison across bases, reflections in the y-axis and the relationship between an exponential and its logarithmic inverse.
questions.methodNote: Use intercepts, simple function values and asymptotic behaviour for the sketches. The key shows the reflection line for the inverse pair in (c).

classification.difficultyReason: Recognise the matching base and rewrite the square-root arguments as fractional powers before applying the supplied identity.

questions.mappingNote: Recognising and evaluating the exponent returned by the logarithm directly assesses its definition.
questions.methodNote: Write the argument as a power of the logarithm base and apply the identity printed in the stem.

classification.difficultyReason: Set each argument strictly above zero and combine that condition with the reciprocal or radical restriction where needed. Recognise that the quadratic argument is always positive.

questions.mappingNote: The positive-argument restriction is part of the logarithm definition. This question applies it to linear, reciprocal, radical and quadratic expressions.
questions.methodNote: Require the argument to be defined and strictly positive, then solve for x.

classification.difficultyReason: Match the outer exponential base with the logarithm base and read off the unchanged argument using the supplied identity.

questions.mappingNote: Each expression reduces to its logarithm argument by the defining inverse relationship.
questions.methodNote: Apply the printed inverse identity to the matching exponential and logarithm bases in each part.

classification.difficultyReason: Part (c) requires recognising 25 as 5² to match the logarithm base, then applying the power law and inverse identity cued by parts (a) and (b).

questions.mappingNote: Part (a) applies the power law, part (b) evaluates the resulting inverse composition, and part (c) first rewrites 25 as a power of 5 to use the same method. The scaffold and follow-up wording supply this sequence.
questions.methodNote: The scaffold shows the coefficient moving inside the logarithm as a power. Part (b) then uses the inverse relationship between exponentiation and logarithms with the same base.

classification.difficultyReason: Apply the positive-argument condition to each logarithm, solve the shifted inequality and identify which restriction determines their intersection.

questions.mappingNote: The sum is defined exactly where both terms are defined. The two arguments in the stem give the separate restrictions, of which $x>2$ is stricter.
questions.methodNote: Require each logarithm argument to be positive and take the common domain.

classification.difficultyReason: Recall the product, quotient and power laws from their displayed forms and complete a cued change-of-base fraction.

questions.mappingNote: The first three printed blanks recall the three laws in order. The final fraction requires the argument in the numerator and the full denominator.
questions.methodNote: Use exponent rules to establish the product, quotient and power laws. For change of base, take logarithms of the exponential form and divide.

classification.difficultyReason: Recognise standard powers of the base and apply the power law directly to a reciprocal and a square root.

questions.mappingNote: The first four blanks ask for specific exponents of the base. The last two ask for equivalent expressions in $\log_a x$.
questions.methodNote: Recognise powers of the base and use the power law with exponents $-1$ and $\frac{1}{2}$.

classification.difficultyReason: Recognise each argument as an exact power of its stated base. The hardest part combines a reciprocal and a square root to identify the exponent −1/2.

questions.mappingNote: The no-calculator stem and ordered arguments assess positive, negative and fractional exponents in the inverse identity.
questions.methodNote: Express the argument as an exact power of the base and read off the exponent.

classification.difficultyReason: Link the quotient law to exact power recognition in the first two parts. In the later parts, evaluate the logarithms and combine their fractional and signed values using the printed operations.

questions.mappingNote: Parts (a) and (b) combine same-base differences. Part (c) multiplies two evaluated values and part (d) subtracts a negative value before adding the final term.
questions.methodNote: Use the quotient law for the two differences. For the other parts, recognise powers of the base and then carry out the printed arithmetic on the logarithm values.

classification.difficultyReason: Apply change of base directly, retain the factor of two where given, and round the final result.

questions.mappingNote: Each item uses a base other than 10. Part (c) retains its factor of 2 until final rounding and part (d) retains the given base below 1.
questions.methodNote: Use the change-of-base rule recalled in Fundamentals 1(d), then round the final value.

classification.difficultyReason: Recognise a nearby integer power of the stated base and read off its exponent, using reciprocal powers for arguments below one.

questions.mappingNote: The shared stem explicitly requires powers of 2, 3 or 10. Arguments below 1 use the corresponding negative powers.
questions.methodNote: Compare each argument with a nearby integer power of its base and use that exponent as the estimate.

classification.difficultyReason: Sequence the logarithm laws for nested quotients, powers and radicals, keeping each sign and coefficient attached to the correct terms before substituting.

questions.mappingNote: The supplied definitions and requested expressions in x, y and z directly assess the laws of logarithms.
questions.methodNote: Expand products, quotients, reciprocals and powers using logarithm laws, then substitute the given logarithms.

classification.difficultyReason: Use the hinted factors to rewrite the arguments, including recognising 6.4 as 2⁵/5, then choose the relevant laws and substitute the given base-five values.

questions.mappingNote: The hint and required expressions in a and b assess expansion using the laws, supported by standard base-5 values.
questions.methodNote: Follow the visible hint by writing the arguments as products, quotients or powers of 2, 3 and 5. Apply the logarithm laws and use log base 5 of 5 equal to 1.

classification.difficultyReason: Students coordinate the power, product and quotient laws. In the hardest part, they must evaluate the different-base logarithm and rewrite its value as a base-5 logarithm before combining.

questions.mappingNote: The stem requires a single logarithm in every part, making the laws the primary skill.
questions.methodNote: Move coefficients into exponents and combine same-base logarithms. In the mixed-base part, evaluate the constant logarithm and express that value as a logarithm of base 5 before combining.

classification.difficultyReason: Students select a law, exact value or counterexample for each decision. The product claim can be rejected by recognising that both logarithms lie between zero and one.

questions.mappingNote: The statements test recognition of logarithm laws, standard values, inverse relationships and change of base.
questions.methodNote: Check numerical statements with exact powers and check symbolic statements using the logarithm laws or change of base. A counterexample suffices to disprove a proposed identity.

classification.difficultyReason: The target base is supplied. Students apply the change-of-base rule and recognise the argument and original base as powers of the target base, including negative powers for the reciprocal bases.

questions.mappingNote: Each bracketed base specifies the method, and the exact evaluation uses inverse logarithmic identities.
questions.methodNote: Apply change of base using the explicitly specified base in both numerator and denominator, then evaluate the logarithms as powers of that base.

classification.difficultyReason: Students choose base b to produce a numerator of one in the proof, then reverse the base and argument using the proved identity and recognise the square root of 27 as a power of 3.

questions.mappingNote: The proof and dependent evaluation directly assess change of base and the resulting reciprocal rule.
questions.methodNote: Prove the reciprocal-logarithm identity by changing to base b and using the logarithm of its own base. Use that reciprocal identity in part (b), as directed by 'Hence'.

classification.difficultyReason: Choose a common base for the three logarithms and recognise that each logarithmic factor occurs once in a numerator and once in a denominator.

questions.mappingNote: The product uses three different bases in cyclic order, so a common base exposes the cancellation.
questions.methodNote: Change to a common base and cancel nonzero factors.

classification.difficultyReason: Choose base a, use the power law to expose the factor x in the numerator and denominator, and recognise that the original base makes x nonzero.

questions.mappingNote: The same exponent occurs in the base and argument, producing a common nonzero factor.
questions.methodNote: Change to base $a$ and use the power law.

classification.difficultyReason: Combine the logarithmic terms to isolate y, then use the original logarithm arguments to identify the domain of the resulting function.

questions.mappingNote: The shared equation asks for a subject change and then the allowed inputs to the resulting function.
questions.methodNote: Use the power and quotient laws, equate arguments, and check positivity in the original logarithms.

classification.difficultyReason: Use the cued squared expression from part (a) to rewrite the logarithm with the power law, then apply the product law to obtain the required half-sum.

questions.mappingNote: The word ‘Hence’ requires the simplified square from part (a) to support the proof in part (b).
questions.methodNote: Expand the square, substitute the given relation, then use the power and product laws.

classification.difficultyReason: Combine the logarithms into a product and recognise that each interior denominator cancels with the next numerator, leaving an exact power of 10.

questions.mappingNote: The displayed sequence of adjacent fractions makes cancellation available after the product law is applied.
questions.methodNote: Combine the sum into one logarithm and cancel the repeated factors in the product.

classification.difficultyReason: Recognise the given quotient as a logarithm to base x and use it as the exponent in the inverse identity.

questions.mappingNote: The given quotient expresses the exponent as a logarithm to the same base as the power.
questions.methodNote: Use change of base followed by the inverse logarithm identity.

classification.difficultyReason: Choose base x from the target expression, expand the product xy inside the denominator logarithm, and simplify log_x(x) to 1.

questions.mappingNote: The product in the original base becomes the sum shown in the target denominator.
questions.methodNote: Change to base $x$, use the product law in the denominator, then use $\log_x(x)=1$.

classification.difficultyReason: Choose base a to expose the denominator log_a(a^x), then use the inverse identity to reduce it to x.

questions.mappingNote: The original base is a power of $a$, so the denominator reduces to the given exponent.
questions.methodNote: Change to base $a$ and simplify the denominator using the inverse identity.

classification.difficultyReason: Part (a) supplies a route to base c. In part (b), students must use that identity in reverse and choose base b for log_c(a) so that the factor log_b(c) cancels.

questions.mappingNote: The first proof rewrites the power with base $c$, allowing the exponent to be simplified to the one requested in the second proof.
questions.methodNote: Use the power-of-a-power rule and the inverse identity in part (a), then change base in the exponent in part (b).

classification.difficultyReason: Complete cued terms from the definition and inverse relationship, and recognise the sign of the natural logarithm on the given interval.

questions.mappingNote: The three sentence completions assess natural-log terminology, the inverse relationship and the sign on (0,1).
questions.methodNote: Use the base-e definition, the inverse identities and the fact that the increasing natural logarithm is zero at 1.

classification.difficultyReason: Complete familiar derivative and inverse identities. The hardest part combines the exponential power law with the inverse identity and supplies the positive-input condition.

questions.mappingNote: The general exponent f(x) in (c) directly assesses the composite rule. Parts (d)–(h) assess base-e notation and positive inputs to the natural logarithm.
questions.methodNote: Differentiate the exponential using the chain rule, then use the definition and inverse identities of the natural logarithm with their domains.

classification.difficultyReason: Apply the same derivative rule to each exponential by reading the signed coefficient of x and multiplying by it.

questions.mappingNote: The four exponents are constant multiples of x, including negative and fractional multiples.
questions.methodNote: Apply the exponential derivative rule elicited by Fundamentals 2, multiplying by the derivative of the exponent.

classification.difficultyReason: Apply the affine-exponent rule directly, identifying the signed slope when the exponent includes a constant or a shared denominator.

questions.mappingNote: All five givens are of the form e^(ax+b), including the two with fractional coefficients and constants.
questions.methodNote: Apply the affine-exponent rule elicited by Fundamentals 2(b), using the coefficient of x as the derivative of the exponent.

classification.difficultyReason: Use index laws to simplify before differentiating. In (f), recognise that splitting the numerator leaves a constant plus a reciprocal exponential.

questions.mappingNote: Each simplification isolates a natural exponential with exponent kx. Part (f) also retains a constant term, whose derivative is zero.
questions.methodNote: The stem specifies simplifying before differentiation. Use index laws and split the fraction in (f), then apply the exponential derivative rule.

classification.difficultyReason: The parts cue the base-e conversion and its use. Students supply the logarithmic exponent, use the power law and differentiate the resulting expression to obtain the stated identity.

questions.mappingNote: The three linked parts directly assess rewriting a base-2 exponential to apply the derivative rule for e^(ax).
questions.methodNote: Follow the printed scaffold: use the inverse identity to rewrite 2, apply the power law to rewrite 2^x, then differentiate the base-e expression.

classification.difficultyReason: Apply the demonstrated base-e conversion to new bases and account for the multiplier in the exponent before differentiating. In (d), the half exponent can also be absorbed by rewriting the base.

questions.mappingNote: All four parts differentiate a constant-base exponential with a linear exponent. The natural logarithm supplies the coefficient when converting to base $e$.
questions.methodNote: Rewrite each power in base $e$, then differentiate using the coefficient of $x$ in the exponent. The answer-book entry immediately before Q5 rewrites $2^x$ as $e^{x\ln 2}$. The preceding student explanation was unavailable.

classification.difficultyReason: Use the supplied inverse identity by moving the logarithm's coefficient outside the exponential as a power, then apply the power rule to the resulting negative, integer or fractional power.

questions.mappingNote: The composite exponential expressions are the differentiation targets, and the supplied natural-logarithm identity determines the solution method.
questions.methodNote: The stem supplies $e^{\ln x}=x$ for $x>0$. Use exponent laws and this identity before differentiating the resulting power of $x$.

classification.difficultyReason: Use the second derivative to identify the repeated factor and justify why differentiating the general mth derivative produces the claimed next derivative.

questions.mappingNote: Both parts apply the linear-exponent derivative rule, first twice and then to justify a factor of $2$ at every step.
questions.methodNote: Differentiate $e^{2x}$ successively. The printed 'Hence' makes the second derivative in (a) the starting example for the general argument in (b).

classification.difficultyReason: Treat P_0 and k as constants, differentiate once with respect to t and recognise the original expression multiplied by k.

questions.mappingNote: The first-order equation directly checks the derivative rule for a constant multiple of an exponential with a linear exponent.
questions.methodNote: Differentiate with respect to $t$, treating $P_0$ and $k$ as constants, then substitute the expression for $P$.

classification.difficultyReason: Differentiate both terms twice, track the sign of the negative-exponent term and recognise that the second derivative reproduces y.

questions.mappingNote: The proof depends on both exponential terms returning to their original form after two differentiations.
questions.methodNote: Differentiate each term twice, then substitute in $y''-y$.

classification.difficultyReason: Find both derivatives, substitute them with y into the weighted equation and collect each exponential term to show that both coefficients vanish.

questions.mappingNote: The equation tests repeated differentiation with different linear exponent coefficients and arbitrary constant multipliers.
questions.methodNote: Find both derivatives, substitute them alongside the given $y$, and collect like exponential terms.

classification.difficultyReason: Differentiate twice with an unknown exponent coefficient, then recognise the common nonzero exponential and reduce the differential equation to a quadratic in that coefficient.

questions.mappingNote: The repeated linear-exponent derivative supplies the factors $k$ and $k^2$ needed to determine the parameter.
questions.methodNote: Differentiate twice, substitute in the equation, divide by the nonzero exponential factor and solve the resulting quadratic.

classification.difficultyReason: Choose a route between the exponential definitions and the products of c and s, then organise the cancellations needed to prove the two-variable addition identities.

questions.mappingNote: Parts (c) and (d) directly assess differentiating $e^x$ and $e^{-x}$. The other parts use the same definitions to establish algebraic identities.
questions.methodNote: Use the supplied definitions with exponent laws and algebra. Differentiate term by term in (c) and (d), and reuse established identities where they shorten later proofs.

classification.difficultyReason: Combine the exponential power law and inverse logarithm identity, then follow the explicit cue to reuse the resulting form and differentiate with a constant inner derivative.

questions.mappingNote: The two-part stem directs students to use the simplification in part (a) to prove the derivative in part (b).
questions.methodNote: Use exponent laws and the inverse identity e^{ln(a)}=a, then differentiate the equivalent exponential with the chain rule.

classification.difficultyReason: After differentiating and substituting, collect terms by exponential and recognise that each resulting coefficient contains the given quadratic evaluated at one of its roots.

questions.mappingNote: The first and second derivatives use the rule for e^{kx}. The given roots explain why both collected terms vanish.
questions.methodNote: Differentiate the two constant-coefficient exponential terms twice, substitute into the differential equation and collect terms by exponential factor.

classification.difficultyReason: Complete three cued rules. The supplied numerator and fraction structure cue the natural-logarithm denominator in the hardest part.

questions.mappingNote: Each scaffold directly cues its rule. The numerator in (c) cues natural logarithms.
questions.methodNote: Use equality of logarithm arguments, equality of exponents and the natural-logarithm power law.

classification.difficultyReason: The stem supplies the common-base method. The hardest parts require absorbing a coefficient into a power or isolating the power before matching exponents.

questions.mappingNote: The stem explicitly requires common bases. In (i), dividing by 4 gives a reciprocal power of 6.
questions.methodNote: Express both sides as powers of a common base and equate the exponents.

classification.difficultyReason: Recognise related bases without an explicit method cue, apply the power law to linear exponent expressions on both sides, then solve the resulting linear equation.

questions.mappingNote: The related bases support the common-base method required by Question 1, now with an expression in each exponent.
questions.methodNote: Rewrite using a common base, equate the exponents and solve the resulting linear equation.

classification.difficultyReason: Choose a common base separately for each equation, recognise the resulting simultaneous linear system, then choose elimination or substitution to find both variables.

questions.mappingNote: Each printed pair supplies two linear expressions in the exponents. The common-base step follows Questions 1 and 2.
questions.methodNote: Use a common base in each equation to obtain a simultaneous linear system, then eliminate or substitute.

classification.difficultyReason: Recognise the quadratic in a positive exponential, including rewriting the shifted exponent in (c), then factor, reject the negative root and solve for x.

questions.mappingNote: Every equation contains an exponential expression and its square. The negative substitution root in each part is outside the exponential range.
questions.methodNote: Substitute a positive exponential expression, factor the resulting quadratic and solve for the exponent.

classification.difficultyReason: Convert a single logarithm to exponential form and solve for its argument or base. In (c), use the positive-base restriction to select the fourth root.

questions.mappingNote: Each part has one logarithm with an unknown argument or base. In (c) the positive-base condition selects the positive fourth root.
questions.methodNote: Rewrite a single logarithm in exponential form and apply the restrictions on the base where it is unknown.

classification.difficultyReason: Choose the applicable logarithm laws, distinguish a squared logarithm from the logarithm of a power, then solve the resulting equations and filter candidates using the original domains.

questions.mappingNote: The question explicitly asks for validity checks. The products, quotient and powers are signalled by the individual equations, and (d) and (e) are directly quadratic in a logarithm.
questions.methodNote: Use the product, quotient or power law as applicable. Substitute the logarithm in (d) and (e) and check candidates against the original logarithm domains.

classification.difficultyReason: Take natural logs as directed, use the power law to bring down the exponent, then divide and round to two decimal places.

questions.mappingNote: The logarithm power law brings down the unknown exponent so it can be isolated.
questions.methodNote: The stem requires taking natural logarithms of both sides.

classification.difficultyReason: The harder parts require choosing an exponent law or factoring out the common exponential, then using positivity to discard impossible values before taking logs.

questions.mappingNote: Each equation is solved by isolating an exponential or showing that its required value is impossible. In the factorable parts, the positive common exponential factor cannot supply a root.
questions.methodNote: Question 7 supplies the natural-logarithm technique. Isolate the exponential first where needed and use its positivity to test for real solutions.

classification.difficultyReason: Recognise the hidden quadratic, rewrite the shifted exponent in the same substitution, then reject a negative quadratic root before recovering the exponent.

questions.mappingNote: The directly assessed step in all three parts is recognising and solving the quadratic form. Natural logarithms recover the non-zero exponent from each surviving root.
questions.methodNote: Each printed equation pairs a base with its square. Substitute the exponential with the smaller base, factor the resulting quadratic, then solve for the exponent.

classification.difficultyReason: Construct the appreciation model, solve for the first doubling time and verify that the second interval is equal by comparing the two growth factors.

questions.mappingNote: The final parts assess solving and comparing doubling intervals in an exponential model. The annual rate sets the base, and elapsed time is the unknown exponent.
questions.methodNote: Form the compound-growth model from the initial value and annual percentage. Use the natural-logarithm method from Question 7 to solve for the time and compare the growth factors.

classification.difficultyReason: Isolate the exponential to solve for the time at a given speed, then use its positivity to justify why the limiting speed is unattainable.

questions.mappingNote: Part (b) directly assesses solving an exponential equation in a model, and part (c) uses the range of the same exponential term to determine whether the stated speed is attainable.
questions.methodNote: Substitute the specified time, then isolate the exponential and use natural logarithms to solve for time. Use positivity of the exponential to justify the limiting speed.

classification.difficultyReason: Use the supplied substitution to form and factor the quadratic, recover both times with logarithms, and interpret the two crossings as absorption and clearance.

questions.mappingNote: The printed scaffold directly requires the reduction to a quadratic and using both roots to solve and interpret the concentration model.
questions.methodNote: Part (b) supplies the exponential substitution. Factor the resulting quadratic, recover both times with natural logarithms, and interpret the two crossings.

classification.difficultyReason: Choose an unstated common base and rewrite a square root or a reciprocal fractional power before equating exponents and solving a linear equation.

questions.mappingNote: All three equations assess common-base rewriting. The source equations support the method choice, and no teaching pages were supplied to verify the textbook's worked sequence.
questions.methodNote: Use a common base and equate exponents. Write the square root as a half power and express the reciprocal power using a negative exponent.

classification.difficultyReason: Build equations from two speed measurements, choose how to eliminate b, use k>0 to reject one quadratic root when fitting the model, and interpret the fitted asymptote as terminal speed.

questions.mappingNote: The question explicitly supplies the substitution, intermediate equation and graphing method. The quadratic substitution is the most advanced equation-solving skill assessed, and recovering $k$ requires solving a simple exponential equation.
questions.methodNote: Substitute the measured speeds, eliminate $b$, solve the quadratic in $p=e^{-k}$, then apply $k>0$ when recovering the constants. Use graphing software to plot the fitted model and interpret its horizontal asymptote.

classification.difficultyReason: Recognise the related bases, choose a common logarithmic base, combine the resulting terms, and convert the solved logarithm back to x.

questions.mappingNote: The bases 8 and 4 are powers of 2, and the resulting equation is linear in $\log_2 x$. No teaching pages were supplied to verify the textbook's preferred method.
questions.methodNote: Rewrite both logarithms in base $2$, solve for $\log_2 x$, and convert to exponential form.

classification.difficultyReason: Sketch two familiar parent graphs by placing their intercepts and showing the direction and asymptote of each curve.

questions.mappingNote: F1(a) and F1(b) are separate sketches. The question and matched answer sketches establish the required method and features.
questions.methodNote: Sketch each parent function from its intercept, monotonicity and limiting behaviour.

classification.difficultyReason: Recall standard features of an exponential graph and select increasing or decreasing for the stated base condition.

questions.mappingNote: The embedded family definition is the shared stem. Parts (a)–(g) independently assess the printed graph properties, with the nonconstant-base condition supplied as a correction.
questions.methodNote: Use the exponential graph and exponent laws to identify the asymptote, domain, range, sign, growth or decay and common intercept.

classification.difficultyReason: Recall the standard logarithmic graph for a base greater than one and use its domain to identify where the expression is undefined.

questions.mappingNote: The shared logarithm definition applies to all six parts. The two separately printed blanks in each of (b) and (c) remain in their owning part.
questions.methodNote: Read the logarithmic graph using its inverse relationship with the increasing exponential graph.

classification.difficultyReason: Read the two tails of the parent exponential and recognise that the negative exponent in part (c) selects the opposite tail.

questions.mappingNote: The three limit directions and the sign of the exponent in part (c) determine the answers in the original three-column order.
questions.methodNote: Read the tails of the exponential graph. For the negative exponent, use the same exponential behaviour with input $-x$.

classification.difficultyReason: Plot the supplied functions and identify the direction and size of the constant vertical shift.

questions.mappingNote: The prompt specifies graphing software and all four translations. The key confirms the shift directions. The solution diagram completes the requested graphical comparison.
questions.methodNote: Plot the four functions on common axes in graphing software and compare their vertical positions.

classification.difficultyReason: Compare the plots to the right of the common intercept and relate the increase in steepness to the larger base.

questions.mappingNote: The question supplies the four bases and the $x>0$ comparison. The key confirms the direction of change in steepness.
questions.methodNote: Plot the four bases on common axes in graphing software and compare the curves to the right of the $y$-axis.

classification.difficultyReason: Recognise that each multiplier scales the curve's height and rise, then describe the resulting change in steepness for positive x.

questions.mappingNote: The five positive values of $k$ in the stem establish a comparison of vertical stretches. The answer uses that comparison and includes the requested family sketch.
questions.methodNote: Use graphing software to plot the positive multiples on common axes and compare their heights and steepness for $x>0$.

classification.difficultyReason: Use the plotted family to connect the sign and magnitude of the exponent offset to the opposite horizontal displacement.

questions.mappingNote: The prompt specifies a software sketch and a comparison of the same base curve under exponent offsets.
questions.methodNote: Plot all five curves together in graphing software and compare horizontal displacement.

classification.difficultyReason: Combine a reflection with a vertical shift, determine whether the transformed curve crosses either axis, and show the resulting shape and intercepts in a sketch.

questions.mappingNote: The nine sketches assess exponent changes, stretches, reflections and translations, with intercepts as the explicit labels.
questions.methodNote: Transform $y=e^x$, substitute $x=0$, and use the curve's position relative to the axes to decide whether it crosses the x-axis.

classification.difficultyReason: Track the positive range through familiar transformations. The most involved part recognises that doubling preserves positivity and a downward shift moves the excluded boundary to −3.

questions.mappingNote: The stem explicitly calls for reasoning from the base graph. Horizontal changes preserve the range, while sign changes and vertical shifts alter it.
questions.methodNote: Start with the range of $y=e^x$ and track changes to the ordinates.

classification.difficultyReason: Differentiate a shifted exponential, solve a specified gradient using logarithms, and combine the sign and limits with the calculated points to sketch the curve. The ordered parts cue each step.

questions.mappingNote: The ordered parts scaffold the final exponential graph. Graphing exponential features is the closest catalogue skill for the combined task.
questions.methodNote: Differentiate with the chain rule and use values, derivative signs and limits to construct the sketch.

classification.difficultyReason: Use reflections and shifts to determine the shape and asymptote, decide whether each curve crosses the x-axis, and solve for the exact crossing where one exists before checking the sketch with software.

questions.mappingNote: The task requires graph features as well as software verification. Exact logarithmic labels are supplied for the two x-intercepts.
questions.methodNote: Sketch by transforming $y=e^{-x}$, determine intercepts and asymptotes, then check each labelled feature with a software plot.

classification.difficultyReason: Translate each named transformation into an input or output change. The hardest part applies two familiar sign changes in an explicitly stated order.

questions.mappingNote: The assessed result is the equation after a translation, reflection or pair of reflections.
questions.methodNote: Apply each transformation to the input or output of $y=e^x$ in the stated order.

classification.difficultyReason: Choose whether each transformation changes the input or output, write the corresponding equation and use software to compare the result with the parent graph on common axes.

questions.mappingNote: Part (b) directly assesses graph transformations. Part (a) supplies the base logarithmic sketch. The method follows the student prompt and the matched answer formulas.
questions.methodNote: Use the intercept, domain and asymptote of the natural logarithm for the base sketch. For each transformation, change the input or output as appropriate and compare the two curves on common axes using graphing software.

classification.difficultyReason: Determine the transformed logarithm’s domain and shape, solve for its exact intercept, and place the intercept and asymptote consistently on the sketch.

questions.mappingNote: The six prompts assess sketching logarithmic graphs and labelling exact intercepts. The method is inferred from the student instructions and the shapes and labels in the six matched answer figures.
questions.methodNote: Use the logarithm's domain, asymptote and transformation to set the shape, then solve y=0 and substitute x=0 when the domain permits it.

classification.difficultyReason: Track the direction of the exponent and carry the resulting growth or decay through a reciprocal or a quotient with a nonzero limiting denominator.

questions.mappingNote: The closest skill is exponential graph features because the seven limits rely on growth and decay at the ends of exponential graphs. The matched answers confirm results; the working is independently derived.
questions.methodNote: Track whether each exponent tends to positive or negative infinity, then apply the corresponding exponential end behaviour to the expression or quotient.

classification.difficultyReason: Recognise that equal heights at the two marked intersections make their x-coordinates solutions, then count the marked points.

questions.mappingNote: The exponential graph skill is the closest catalogue fit for interpreting the intersection of the exponential with a line. The student diagram supplies the graphical method and the keyed answer confirms it.
questions.methodNote: Read solutions graphically as the abscissas where the two graphs share a y-value, then count the intersections.

classification.difficultyReason: Use the fixed logarithmic graph to decide which expression to isolate, then turn the rearranged right-hand side into the comparison function. The hardest parts require moving a factor of x across the equation.

questions.mappingNote: The question supplies y = ln(x) as the fixed curve in all four parts. The closest catalogue skill is graph-log-functions.
questions.methodNote: Isolate ln(x), then graph the expression on the other side.

classification.difficultyReason: Sketch familiar parent curves and use their increasing shape to turn the given left-to-right order of the inputs into a comparison of output heights.

questions.mappingNote: Part (a) assesses exponential behaviour. Part (b) extends the same graphical comparison to the natural logarithm on its positive domain.
questions.methodNote: Use each graph's increasing shape to compare the heights above the two inputs.

classification.difficultyReason: Sketch a translated exponential and a line on the same axes, then rearrange the equation and use the relative positions and shapes of the graphs to justify exactly two solutions.

questions.mappingNote: Part (a) establishes the exponential's features. Part (b) adds the comparison line to the same sketch. Part (c) explicitly asks for the graphical justification.
questions.methodNote: Sketch the translated exponential and straight line on common axes and use the intersections to count solutions.

classification.difficultyReason: Compare software plots, then use the supplied change-of-base hint to identify a decreasing positive multiplier and explain why it makes the curves flatter.

questions.mappingNote: The task moves from plotting a family and describing its shape to justifying the shape change using the printed hint.
questions.methodNote: Compare the four logarithmic graphs, then use change of base to express each as a vertical scaling of ln(x).

classification.difficultyReason: Recognise the uncued quadratic structure in 2^x, solve the resulting quadratic and use positivity to reject the inadmissible root before converting back to x.

questions.mappingNote: The closest available exponential skill covers properties of powers and positivity. The task applies them to an equation.
questions.methodNote: Use the common base to substitute a positive variable and factor the resulting quadratic.

classification.difficultyReason: Follow the ordered cues to extract parameters from the asymptote and two points, then verify the exact crossing by combining a negative exponent with the inverse logarithm identity.

questions.mappingNote: The primary skill covers the asymptote and intercepts of a shifted exponential. The intercept check also uses the inverse relationship.
questions.methodNote: Follow the printed sequence: read the asymptote, substitute the two points and check the marked intercept using the inverse relation between powers and logarithms.

classification.difficultyReason: Use the hint to choose a power that clears both radicals, then use positivity to infer the original order from the resulting integers.

questions.mappingNote: The available exponential skill is the closest fit to manipulating and comparing powers. The directly assessed operation is comparison using rational indices.
questions.methodNote: Use the common-power comparison directed by the printed hint. The sixth power removes both radicals and preserves order for positive inputs.

classification.difficultyReason: Identify the growing exponential as the common divisor, rewrite the quotient in terms of a decaying exponential, and evaluate the resulting limit.

questions.mappingNote: Exponential end behaviour is the closest available skill and is the property needed to evaluate this limit.
questions.methodNote: Divide through by the growing exponential and use the limiting behaviour of the resulting decaying exponential.

classification.difficultyReason: Simplify the logarithms to zero and carry the original domain through to a ray with an excluded endpoint.

questions.mappingNote: The logarithmic graph skill is the closest fit because the logarithm domain determines the visible portion of the simplified graph.
questions.methodNote: Simplify first as requested, then sketch on the original logarithmic domain.

classification.difficultyReason: Trace the supplied proof to locate the invalid division, infer that the logarithmic divisor is negative by comparing its input with 1, and explain why the inequality reverses.

questions.mappingNote: The supplied proof isolates the sign of the logarithm as the decisive feature. The closest catalogue skill is graph-log-functions because it covers increasing behaviour of logarithmic functions. The question itself requires no graph.
questions.methodNote: Use the increasing logarithm and its value at 1 to determine the sign of the divisor. Apply the rule that division by a negative number reverses an inequality.

classification.difficultyReason: Use k > 0 to identify the vanishing exponential and carry its zero limit into the two expressions with constants.

questions.mappingNote: The printed condition k > 0 and the order of the four expressions support this method. The exercise teaching pages were unavailable.
questions.methodNote: Express a negative exponential as a reciprocal. For positive k its limit is zero, then apply the limit to each expression involving constants.

classification.difficultyReason: Recall the elapsed-time domain and substitute t = 0, using e^0 = 1 in each supplied model.

questions.mappingNote: The printed prompts identify the starting time and explicitly require evaluation at t = 0 in the three models. The exercise teaching pages were unavailable.
questions.methodNote: Measure time from the start of the model and evaluate each initial value by substituting t = 0 and using e^0 = 1.

classification.difficultyReason: Select the derivative inequality that guarantees each stated direction of change over the given interval.

questions.mappingNote: The paired statements ask for conditions that ensure increase or decrease throughout the time domain. Growth and decay analysis is the closest supplied skill. The exercise teaching pages were unavailable.
questions.methodNote: Use the sign of the derivative throughout the interval to establish whether the function increases or decreases.

classification.difficultyReason: Translate appreciation and depreciation into annual multipliers and generalise the repeated multiplication to a symbolic rate over n years.

questions.mappingNote: The initial value, annual changes and common time horizon make these appreciation and depreciation tasks direct applications of compound percentage change. The exercise teaching pages were unavailable.
questions.methodNote: Convert the percentage to a fraction of the current value, form the annual multiplier and apply it n times.

classification.difficultyReason: The early parts scaffold the annual multiplier and model. The final part requires setting up a logarithmic threshold equation and identifying the year containing the crossing.

questions.mappingNote: The car's first two values lead directly to the general depreciation formula, the retained percentage and the threshold year.
questions.methodNote: Apply the annual multiplier 0.9 repeatedly, then solve the threshold equation using logarithms. The Exercise 8F F4(b) answer on teacher PDF page 72 corroborates the depreciation multiplier.

classification.difficultyReason: Students construct a growth model from the percentage and initial count, then identify the first integer elapsed time satisfying the threshold and convert it to a calendar year.

questions.mappingNote: The enrolment is observed at the beginning of each calendar year, so the elapsed year count is measured from the beginning of 2000.
questions.methodNote: Use the annual multiplier 1.2 and solve the threshold inequality for an integer number of elapsed years. The F4(c) key on teacher PDF page 72 corroborates the general percentage-growth formula.

classification.difficultyReason: Students use two observations to determine the model parameters, with the target value of k supplied, then reuse the fitted model to solve and interpret a logarithmic threshold inequality.

questions.mappingNote: The observations determine A and k, which then give the four-week prediction and the million-ant threshold.
questions.methodNote: Substitute the initial value at t = 0, use the second observation to isolate the exponential and take natural logarithms. The source show-that value establishes the intended exact parameter.

classification.difficultyReason: Students fit a decay model with the target value of k supplied, handle the negative exponent when solving the extinction inequality, and select the first year-end strictly below the cutoff.

questions.mappingNote: The decay model gives the ten-year population and, with the question's explicit definition of extinction, the time when the population falls below one.
questions.methodNote: Substitute the two observations to find A₀ and isolate the exponential. Take natural logarithms, keeping the negative exponent or its reciprocal explicit.

classification.difficultyReason: Convert elapsed hours to doubling periods, use the resulting exponent in a threshold inequality, and convert the logarithmic result to minutes.

questions.mappingNote: Repeated doubling and a model in elapsed hours directly assess exponential growth. Part (c) additionally assesses solving an exponential inequality.
questions.methodNote: Use the number of half-hour periods as the exponent of 2, then solve the threshold inequality using logarithms. The parts and rounding request indicate a continuous time model.

classification.difficultyReason: Apply the stated doubling rule and reverse it by recognising the target-to-initial thickness ratio as a power of two.

questions.mappingNote: The fold count is the discrete exponent in a doubling model, with direct and inverse calculations in the two parts.
questions.methodNote: Multiply the initial thickness by 2 for each fold. Express the thickness ratio as a power of 2 to find the number of folds.

classification.difficultyReason: Establish a reflection identity by rewriting the exponential fraction, then connect that relationship and the software sketch to the vertical shift that centres the symmetry at the origin.

questions.mappingNote: Interpreting the intercept and symmetry of an exponential-based function is the closest available skill. The function is shared across both parts.
questions.methodNote: Use a common denominator for the identity, then use the software sketch to identify the centre of symmetry and verify the translation using the identity. The proof method in the full worked solutions is unavailable.

classification.difficultyReason: Use the derivative to obtain and sketch the tangent, then construct the perpendicular normal and use line intercepts to identify the base and height of each triangle.

questions.mappingNote: Graph and intercept interpretation is the nearest available skill. The supplied taxonomy has no direct differentiation, tangent, normal or area skill.
questions.methodNote: Differentiate to obtain the tangent gradient, sketch the curve and tangent, then use line intercepts and the perpendicular gradient to calculate the areas.

classification.difficultyReason: Form two equations from nonzero times, recognise that their ratio eliminates the unknown multiplier, then use a logarithm and substitute back.

questions.mappingNote: Fitting an exponential population model is the main task. Logarithms determine the growth constant exactly.
questions.methodNote: Substitute both observations, divide to eliminate the initial population, solve for the rate using logarithms and substitute back for the initial population.

classification.difficultyReason: Extend the numerical rewrite to symbolic parameters by separating the constant exponent and identifying which factors determine the new multiplier and base.

questions.mappingNote: Normalising exponential expressions into the model form is the nearest catalogue skill. Neither part asks for an unknown exponent.
questions.methodNote: Use the product and power laws of indices to put the constant factor and the base into standard exponential form.

classification.difficultyReason: Turn each point pair into equations, eliminate the multiplier to recover the positive base, and use the intercept directly when a point has x=0.

questions.mappingNote: Each part constructs an exponential model from a pair of points. The unknown base is determined by a root of a fixed power.
questions.methodNote: Substitute the point coordinates and divide the equations to isolate a power of the base. At an intercept with $x=0$, read the multiplier directly from $a^0=1$.

classification.difficultyReason: Choose the restriction for each function type, then exclude an exponential denominator zero or solve a linear positivity inequality.

questions.mappingNote: The closest available skill covers finding the exponential denominator's zero and solving the algebraic restrictions on logarithms.
questions.methodNote: Exclude real zeros of denominators and solve the positive-argument condition for each logarithm.

classification.difficultyReason: Apply the positivity condition to x², then connect the two branches of a software plot and the break at zero to the algebraic domain.

questions.mappingNote: The logarithmic domain condition and the graph verification are the direct tasks. The exponential and logarithmic equations skill is the closest supplied catalogue entry.
questions.methodNote: Apply the positive-argument condition for the natural logarithm, then verify the domain using graphing software as explicitly directed.

classification.difficultyReason: Set the remaining mass to half the original mass, cancel the original mass, then solve logarithmically and explain why only k determines the half-life.

questions.mappingNote: The proof concerns a quantity derived from an exponential decay model. Solving the exponential equation is an intermediate skill.
questions.methodNote: Use the definition and the model given in the stem. Set the remaining mass to half the original mass, cancel the common factor and take natural logarithms.

classification.difficultyReason: Find the threshold crossing by solving the supplied decay model with logarithms, then use its decreasing behaviour to identify which times satisfy the strict inequality before rounding.

questions.mappingNote: Both parts assess analysis of the supplied exponential decay model. Part (b) also directly assesses solving an exponential equation.
questions.methodNote: Use the half-life model and the example embedded in the stem. Substitute the given time in part (a). In part (b), solve the threshold equation with logarithms and use the decreasing model to interpret when the mass is below the threshold.

classification.difficultyReason: The parts cue differentiation and tangent construction. The student then uses the origin as a point on the tangent and cancels the nonzero exponential factor to locate the contact point.

questions.mappingNote: The central task is exponential differentiation and tangent construction. The closest supplied skill is solving the equation containing the exponential factor that arises from the origin condition.
questions.methodNote: Differentiate the exponential, use point–gradient form and substitute the origin into the resulting tangent equation. The part sequence and teacher answer form support this method.

classification.difficultyReason: Choose a common logarithm base and expose the factor from 9 = 3² so the logarithms cancel. The remaining parts use direct recognition of powers.

questions.mappingNote: The exact simplification of logarithms with different bases is the main task. Part (a) also uses the power law, and parts (b) and (c) use index–log conversion. The chapter's teaching sequence could not be verified.
questions.methodNote: Apply the power law and change of base in part (a), then evaluate logarithms by recognising powers in parts (b) and (c).

classification.difficultyReason: Find the two intercepts, use the exponential intercept's height to locate a point on the logarithmic curve, then follow the guides and use coordinate differences to find the area.

questions.mappingNote: The supplied figure governs the coordinate reasoning. The logarithmic curve supplies D and B, and the exponential curve supplies A. The chapter's presentation of these methods could not be verified.
questions.methodNote: Use the plotted intercepts, convert logarithmic statements to index form and follow the dashed projections. Subtract the corresponding coordinates to obtain the rectangle's dimensions.

classification.difficultyReason: Recognise the root and reciprocal as powers, then multiply the given logarithm by the exponent in each part.

questions.mappingNote: Every part tests extracting an exponent from a logarithm. The reciprocal in part (c) also tests the standard negative-log result. The chapter's preferred derivation could not be verified.
questions.methodNote: Use powers of p in all four parts, rewriting the square root and reciprocal as powers before applying the power law and substituting 1.6.

classification.difficultyReason: The harder part requires treating the square root as a power, expanding the product and the inner power, then substituting the given logarithms.

questions.mappingNote: Both parts directly assess expanding logarithms to isolate the given arguments a, b and c. The chapter's worked order could not be verified.
questions.methodNote: Apply the quotient and power laws in part (a), and the power and product laws in part (b). Substitute the shared definitions after expansion.

classification.difficultyReason: The hint cues rewriting 2 as a natural logarithm. The student must supply e², simplify and combine the logarithms, then invert the logarithm to isolate y.

questions.mappingNote: The visible hint establishes the first step. Simplifying the logarithms is the main assessed skill.
questions.methodNote: Use the embedded hint to rewrite 2 as a natural logarithm, apply the logarithm laws and exponentiate.

classification.difficultyReason: The student must recognise that combining the logarithms and exponentiating exposes a quadratic, then use the original domain to select the admissible root before rounding.

questions.mappingNote: The product law produces a quadratic, and the requested precision applies only to the admissible root.
questions.methodNote: Combine the logarithms, convert to exponential form, solve the resulting quadratic and check the roots against the original domain before rounding.

classification.difficultyReason: Apply the positive-argument condition directly, solving a linear inequality in one part and recognising that a square plus one is always positive in the other.

questions.mappingNote: The closest catalogue skill covers the domain of a logarithmic function. Both parts assess domain directly.
questions.methodNote: Require each logarithm argument to be positive. Solve the linear inequality in (a) and use the non-negativity of a square in (b).

classification.difficultyReason: Rewrite the numerator and denominator as powers of the given arguments, then combine the quotient and power laws to express the result in a and b.

questions.mappingNote: The shared definitions govern all four parts. Part (c) also accepts a form using the logarithm of the base.
questions.methodNote: Rewrite arguments as products, quotients or powers involving 3 and 4. Use the logarithm laws and substitute the given expressions.

classification.difficultyReason: Interpret the changes to the natural-log graph, preserve its vertical asymptote and determine the exact intercepts before sketching.

questions.mappingNote: The three prompts directly assess graph sketches. The answer-book curves verify the required shapes and intercepts. They do not specify a worked construction method.
questions.methodNote: Transform the base natural-logarithm graph, retain its vertical asymptote and calculate the intercepts and any labelled points.

classification.difficultyReason: Use the intercept and horizontal guide to solve for two exact x-coordinates, then read the perpendicular height and subtract the x-coordinates to obtain the base.

questions.mappingNote: The supplied graph determines the two exact x-coordinates. Its guides and right-angle marker determine which lengths give the area.
questions.methodNote: Use the curve's intercept and the horizontal guide to find the required coordinates. Read off the perpendicular base and height and apply the triangle area formula.

classification.difficultyReason: Verify the given factorisation by expansion and index laws, then set each factor to zero and solve both resulting equations using base 3.

questions.mappingNote: The word “Hence” makes the factorisation from (a) the required starting point for (b). The two parts form one equation-solving task.
questions.methodNote: Verify the supplied factorisation by expansion and index laws, then use it to solve by the zero-product rule and common bases.

classification.difficultyReason: Recognise the repeated logarithm as a single variable, factor the resulting quadratic and invert the logarithm for each root.

questions.mappingNote: The squared logarithm and the linear logarithm term directly assess an equation quadratic in a logarithm.
questions.methodNote: Substitute for the natural logarithm, factor the resulting quadratic and exponentiate to recover the positive solutions.

classification.difficultyReason: Recognise the negative exponential as a reciprocal, clear it using the positive exponential, then identify a perfect-square quadratic and solve for the exponent.

questions.mappingNote: The reciprocal exponential term reduces to a quadratic in $e^x$, making quadratic-form exponential equations the closest directly assessed skill.
questions.methodNote: The authored solution clears the reciprocal by multiplying by the positive quantity $e^x$, then factorises a quadratic in $e^x$. The textbook's taught sequence is unverified.

classification.difficultyReason: Use the asymptote to determine the vertical shift, use the intercept to isolate the multiplier, then use the negative-input point to determine the base before evaluating the function at −3.

questions.mappingNote: Reading the asymptote and intercept of a shifted exponential is essential to part (a). Part (b) evaluates the same function.
questions.methodNote: The supplied graph gives the asymptote. Use it and the y-intercept to find c and k, substitute the other known point to find a, then evaluate the function at x=-3. No teaching pages were supplied for comparison.

classification.difficultyReason: Recognise ln(x) and its reciprocal as expressions in one unknown, clear the denominator subject to the original domain, solve the quadratic and convert both roots back to values of x.

questions.mappingNote: Part (d) directly assesses solving a quadratic in ln(x). The preceding parts assess logarithm laws, equation solving and domain checks.
questions.methodNote: The authored solutions use the power or product law and the original domain in parts (a)–(c), and a quadratic substitution in part (d). No teaching pages were supplied for comparison.

classification.difficultyReason: Recognise that taking reciprocals lets both denominator terms use base x, combine them with the product law, then convert the outer reciprocal to a logarithm in base ab.

questions.mappingNote: Change of base handles the reciprocal logarithms, and the product law explains the resulting base ab.
questions.methodNote: The authored proof changes both reciprocal logarithms to base x, applies the product law, then changes base again. No teaching pages were supplied for comparison.

classification.difficultyReason: Translate compounding frequencies into periods per year, apply the supplied formula, and interpret the balances as evidence of a limiting value.

questions.mappingNote: Students substitute five compounding frequencies into the given model and interpret the resulting balances.
questions.methodNote: The common prompt defines the discrete compound interest model.

classification.difficultyReason: Evaluate a supplied expression at tabulated inputs and recognise e from the resulting numerical pattern.

questions.mappingNote: Students use the numerical pattern to recognise $e$ before using the limit in Question 3.
questions.methodNote: The table asks students to evaluate the same power at four increasing values of $x$.

classification.difficultyReason: Choose a workable linear intensity scale, construct a logarithmic curve, and combine a direct evaluation and an inverse calculation with an interpretation of the scale.

questions.mappingNote: Constructing and interpreting the logarithmic graph is the main skill. Part (c) also requires solving a logarithmic equation.
questions.methodNote: The embedded introduction supplies the base-10 logarithmic model and its reference intensity. Use it to find graph points, substitute for a sound level and convert to index form to find an intensity.

classification.difficultyReason: Recognise that the common reference cancels when comparing two levels, use the quotient law to connect a level difference to an intensity ratio, and reverse that relationship for the shuttle comparison.

questions.mappingNote: Parts (a) and (b) assess the logarithm quotient law through a comparison of sound levels and intensities. Part (b) also converts a logarithmic equation to index form.
questions.methodNote: The embedded model relates a decibel level to the logarithm of an intensity ratio. Subtracting two levels and applying the quotient law cancels the common reference intensity. Direct substitution gives the three levels for the threshold comparison.

classification.difficultyReason: Choose a usable concentration scale and turn the supplied reciprocal logarithm into a sketch with the correct intercept, asymptote and direction.

questions.mappingNote: The prompt restates the formula and units so the graphing task has its own givens. The solution uses the base-10 logarithm to identify points and end behaviour on linear axes.
questions.methodNote: The supplied formula specifies pH as a function of positive hydronium ion concentration. The page specifies no particular graphing procedure or scale.

classification.difficultyReason: Identify the highest reported pH as the least acidic reference, invert the logarithmic model for each sample and express the comparisons as concentration ratios relative to that reference.

questions.mappingNote: The prompt restates the model for independent use. The solution derives the concentration ratio from two pH values and illustrates the ranking with conditional sample data.
questions.methodNote: The embedded base-10 model relates pH to hydronium ion concentration. The reference is selected by pH.
